title: WORKING WITH INTELLIGENCE
subtitle: The Professional's Complete Guide to AI — Prompting, Projects, Agents, and Playbooks for Every Industry
author: Tang Shiuan Jenn

content_policy.no_invented_evidence: No invented statistics, studies, surveys, percentages, adoption rates, ROI figures, salary data, or job-loss numbers ANYWHERE. If a claim would need a citation, either state it as a general observation or leave it out. Never write 'studies show', 'research proves', or 'X% of companies'.
content_policy.no_fake_cases: No fabricated case studies and no named real company doing a specific thing. Illustrative scenarios are allowed only when clearly generic and clearly labelled as illustrative ('imagine a mid-sized insurer').
content_policy.no_promises: No income promises, no guaranteed savings, no 'this will make you indispensable'. Benefits are described as possible and conditional.
content_policy.product_facts: Describe AI products by durable capability, not version numbers or prices. Where a product is named (Claude, Claude Code, Claude Projects, ChatGPT, Copilot, Gemini, MCP), describe what the category does and add that details change and readers should check current documentation. No vendor endorsement, no affiliate framing, no claims about any vendor's internal data.
content_policy.not_advice: Legal, tax, medical, and regulatory content is general information only, never advice; every such chapter says so plainly and tells the reader to check their own jurisdiction, regulator, employer policy, and professional body.
content_policy.honesty_about_limits: Every capability claim is paired with its limit. The book's credibility rests on saying plainly what AI cannot do and when not to use it.
content_policy.author_bio: The author is described as a qualified chartered accountant (a factual credential) who works with AI systems daily. Do NOT claim an academic degree in AI, vendor certification, employment by any AI company, or any consulting engagement that has not happened.
content_policy.author_anecdotes: OPENINGS: do NOT write first-person anecdotes that claim specific experiences for the author ('I once watched...', 'a colleague sent me...', 'I sat through...'). The author cannot verify or own invented memories, and the book's credibility depends on not manufacturing them. Open instead with: a second-person scene the reader recognises ('It is twenty past ten on a Thursday night and...'), a generic professional situation ('Picture someone trying to...'), a direct question, or a plain observation about how the work actually goes. First-person 'I' is permitted only sparingly, for the author's stated professional STANCE or judgement ('I would fight to keep that constraint'), never for a claimed event, and never involving a named or identifiable person, client, or firm.

style_rules.voice: Second person, direct, warm, unhurried. A senior colleague explaining something useful over coffee — never a hype merchant, never a lecturer. Short sentences carry the important points. British-Malaysian professional English.
style_rules.openings: Every chapter opens with a concrete scene or a specific question a working person actually has — never 'In today's fast-paced world'.
style_rules.structure: Each chapter: opening scene, the idea, how it works, worked examples with real prompt text, what to watch for, and a short 'Do this today' close.
style_rules.prompts: Prompt examples are shown as indented blocks introduced by a line ending in a colon, in the six-part frame from ch09 wherever practical.
style_rules.tables: At least one genuine table per chapter where the material supports it. Tables use the pipe format.
style_rules.no_products: The book never mentions the author's other books or any URL.

chapters.title: The Five-Minute Mental Model

art.title: What actually happens when you press Enter

chapters.brief: The foundation chapter. What a large language model actually does: predicts the next piece of text, over and over, at enormous scale. No database lookup, no search of a filing cabinet, no understanding in the human sense — and yet genuinely useful. Kill the two opposite myths in one chapter: it is not a magic oracle, and it is not 'just autocomplete' in the dismissive sense. End with why this single mental model predicts almost every strength and every failure in the rest of the book.
chapters.tables: one table: What it is / What it is not

chapters.title: From Software You Instruct to Software You Converse With

art.title: Two eras of using a computer
labels: TRADITIONAL SOFTWARE|Exact commands|Fails loudly|Same input, same output|You adapt to it
AI SYSTEMS|Natural language|Fails quietly|Same input, varied output|It adapts to you

chapters.brief: Why this technology feels different from every tool the reader has used. Deterministic software versus probabilistic systems. The professional consequences: you can no longer test once and trust forever; you must verify. Introduce the book's spine — fluency is a skill, not a purchase.

chapters.title: The Capability Map: What It Is Genuinely Good At

art.title: Where AI earns its keep
labels: SWEET SPOT: drafting, summarising, translating, restructuring

chapters.brief: An honest capability map built on the ch01 model. Strong: language transformation, summarising, drafting, explaining, restructuring, classification, first-pass analysis. Weak: arithmetic reliability, current facts, private facts, its own certainty, anything requiring accountability. Give the reader a test they can apply to any new task in 10 seconds.

chapters.title: Hallucination: Why Fluency Is Not Knowledge

art.title: Anatomy of a confident wrong answer

chapters.brief: The single most important professional risk chapter. Why a model generates false things in the same voice as true things, why it invents citations and figures, and why confidence is not correlated with accuracy. Practical detection: which categories of claim to distrust by default. The Three-Check Rule introduced here and used throughout the book.

chapters.title: Context Is Everything

art.title: The four layers the model can actually see

chapters.brief: The concept that explains most user frustration. What the context window is, why the model 'forgets', why a long chat degrades, why it cannot see the file you did not attach or the meeting you did not describe. Practical: what to put in context and what to leave out; context as the reader's main lever of control.

chapters.title: Tokens, Cost, and Speed: The Physics of the Thing

art.title: Where the money and the seconds go

chapters.brief: Demystify tokens, pricing per million tokens, and why long documents cost more and take longer. Cover reasoning/thinking modes as a cost-quality dial. Practical budgeting for a professional or small firm: which work justifies the slow expensive setting and which does not. Use ranges and principles, never invented vendor prices.
chapters.tables: table: task type vs recommended setting

chapters.title: The Model Zoo: Telling the Tools Apart
chapters.brief: A field guide to the categories a professional will meet — chat assistants, reasoning models, multimodal, embeddings/search, generators, coding agents — described by what they DO, not by brand or version, so the chapter stays true as products change. How to read a model's stated context window and capabilities. One page on how fast this field moves and how to check current facts rather than trusting a book's version numbers.

chapters.title: What Must Never Go In: Confidentiality and Professional Duty
chapters.brief: The professional's red-line chapter, written for people with duties of confidentiality — accountants, lawyers, doctors, HR, bankers. How consumer chat, business tiers, and enterprise deployments differ in what happens to your data. Redaction and anonymisation as a working habit. Written as general professional guidance, not legal advice: readers must check their own regulator, employer policy, and engagement terms.
chapters.tables: table: deployment type vs data handling questions to ask

chapters.title: The Anatomy of a Good Prompt

art.title: The six parts of a prompt that works

chapters.brief: The book's core teaching chapter. Introduce the six-part frame and build one real professional prompt from a one-line wish to a working instruction, showing the output improving at each step. This frame is referenced by every later chapter and the industry playbooks.
chapters.tables: before/after table of the same prompt at three levels

chapters.title: Specificity: The Difference Between a Wish and an Instruction

art.title: Wish versus instruction
labels: WISH|'Summarise this report'|'Make it professional'|'Analyse the numbers'|'Write something about AI'

INSTRUCTION|'Summarise in 200 words for a non-financial board member, five bullets, flag any figure you are unsure of'|'Rewrite in plain formal English, no exclamation marks, Malaysian business register'|'List the three largest variances and what each would cost'|'Write a 600-word briefing for staff on our new AI policy'

chapters.brief: Teach precision. The five dimensions of specificity: audience, length, tone, scope, and success criteria. Why vague prompts produce generic writing, and why 'be more professional' fails while a named register succeeds.

chapters.title: Show, Don't Tell: Examples and Patterns
chapters.brief: Few-shot prompting for non-technical readers: give it two or three examples of what you want and it will match them better than any description. Practical uses: matching house style, standard email replies, consistent categorisation. When examples hurt (too narrow, contradictory, biased).

chapters.title: Give It a Shape: Formats, Tables, and Schemas

art.title: Asking for the output you can actually use

chapters.brief: How specifying the output shape improves both usability and accuracy. Asking for tables with named columns, for a fixed template, for a machine-readable format. Why a defined shape reduces waffle and makes verification faster.
chapters.tables: table: output format vs when to use it

chapters.title: Make It Think Before It Answers

art.title: Plan, draft, check
labels: Ask it to check its own work

chapters.brief: The highest-leverage habit in the book: separating thinking from answering. Ask for an approach before the deliverable; ask for reasoning steps on analytical work; use reasoning modes where available. Why this reduces (not eliminates) errors, and why you must still verify.

chapters.title: The Critique Loop: Making AI Grade Its Own Work
chapters.brief: Teach the loop that turns a mediocre first draft into a strong final one: draft, then critique with explicit criteria, then revise, then verify. Include prompt patterns for 'attack this as a hostile reviewer' and 'list what is missing'. Be honest about the ceiling: a model cannot catch what it does not know.

chapters.title: Voice, Persona, and House Style
chapters.brief: How to make AI write in your voice or your firm's. Building a reusable style instruction from samples of your own writing. Where personas genuinely help (audience-shifting, explaining to a lay reader) and where they are theatre.

chapters.title: Working With Long Documents
chapters.brief: Contracts, annual reports, policy manuals, transcripts. Chunking, hierarchical summarising, extraction into tables, and the crucial habit of verifying extracted figures against the source page. Why 'summarise this 200-page document' in one shot is the wrong instruction.

chapters.title: Twelve Ways It Goes Wrong, and the Fix for Each
chapters.brief: A diagnostic chapter organised as a clinic: the symptom, the cause in terms of the ch01 model, and the specific fix. Include sycophancy — the model agreeing with a wrong premise — and how to prompt against it.
chapters.tables: big diagnostic table: symptom / likely cause / fix

chapters.title: The Professional Prompt Library

art.title: Forty prompts you will actually reuse

chapters.brief: A large reference chapter: roughly forty ready-to-use prompts across eight professional categories, each written in the six-part frame, each with a one-line note on what to check in the output. Written so a reader can copy, adapt, and keep.
chapters.tables: prompts presented as labelled blocks with usage notes

chapters.title: Projects: Giving AI a Permanent Workspace
chapters.brief: The step most users never take. A project (Claude Projects and equivalents) keeps instructions and reference material permanently in context so you stop re-explaining yourself. How to design one: what belongs in instructions versus knowledge. Worked example: a month-end close project, an engagement project, a policy-drafting project. Describe capabilities durably; note that product details change and readers should check current documentation.

chapters.title: Knowledge and Retrieval Without the Jargon

art.title: How AI searches your own documents

chapters.brief: Retrieval explained for non-technical readers: why attaching your own documents beats hoping the model 'knows', how semantic search differs from keyword search, and why retrieval reduces but does not eliminate invention. When a project is enough and when a proper retrieval system is warranted.

chapters.title: Standing Instructions and the House Manual

art.title: One page that improves every answer

chapters.brief: Writing the personal or firm-level standing instruction: the single page that makes every future conversation better. Include a full worked example for a finance professional and one for a small business owner.

chapters.title: What 'Agentic' Actually Means
chapters.brief: Demystify agents: a model in a loop with tools and a goal. The four honest questions before building one — is the task hard to specify in advance, is the value worth the cost, is the model capable, can errors be caught and reversed. Why most work should NOT be an agent.

chapters.title: Tools: How AI Reaches the Outside World
chapters.brief: Tool use explained plainly: the model asks for an action, something else performs it, the result comes back. Introduce MCP as the emerging standard plug — a common way to connect assistants to systems — described conceptually, since implementations move fast. Security implications of giving an assistant hands.

chapters.title: Claude Code and the Rise of the Working Assistant

art.title: AI that works in your files

chapters.brief: A whole chapter on the category that surprises non-programmers most: assistants that operate on real files and run real commands. What Claude Code actually is, what it is genuinely good at beyond programming (data cleaning, document generation, repetitive file work, analysis pipelines), and how a non-programmer can use it safely. Emphasise review-before-apply and reversibility. Keep to durable behaviour, not version specifics.

chapters.title: Automation: When to Hand Over the Wheel
chapters.brief: The decision framework for moving from assistance to automation, scheduled runs, and pipelines. The reversibility test. Designing the human checkpoint. Failure modes of unattended automation and how to notice them early.

chapters.title: Many Hands: Multi-Agent Patterns
chapters.brief: The patterns that genuinely improve quality: splitting work across parallel workers, an independent reviewer, an adversarial verifier, a judge panel for hard choices. Presented so a reader can apply the same patterns manually, with no code, using separate chats or windows.

chapters.title: Choosing Your Setup
chapters.brief: A decision tree that closes Part III: chat, project, knowledge base, working assistant, agent, or custom build. Cost, effort, control, and risk compared honestly.
chapters.tables: table: surface vs setup effort vs control vs typical cost

parts.title: Making AI Better at Your Work

chapters.title: Write the Test First: How to Know It Is Any Good
chapters.brief: Bring engineering discipline to everyday use: define what good looks like before you prompt, keep a small set of real test cases, and re-run them when you change anything. The single habit that separates professionals from dabblers.

chapters.title: Grounding: Give It the Truth to Work From

art.title: Ungrounded versus grounded
labels: UNGROUNDED|Answers from training|Invents specifics|Cannot cite|Confident either way
GROUNDED|Answers from your documents|Quotes real passages|Can cite the source|Says when it cannot find it

chapters.brief: The most reliable single upgrade: stop asking the model what it knows, start giving it what it must use. Practical grounding methods for professionals — attach the standard, paste the clause, supply the file, require quotation with page references.

chapters.title: The Three-Check Rule

art.title: Verification that fits in a working day

chapters.brief: A verification discipline light enough that people actually do it. What to check always, what to check by sampling, and what to trust. Includes a short verification checklist for financial, legal, and factual output.

chapters.title: Iteration: Getting to Good in Four Turns
chapters.brief: Most people accept the first answer or start over. Teach the disciplined middle path: name the specific gap, add one constraint at a time, and keep the version that worked. Include how to save and reuse the winning prompt.

chapters.title: Prompting, Retrieval, or Training: Which Lever
chapters.brief: How to choose the cheapest lever that solves the problem. When fine-tuning is genuinely warranted (rare for most professionals) and when it is an expensive way to avoid writing a better prompt.
chapters.tables: table: symptom vs correct lever

chapters.title: Your Personal AI System

art.title: The four things to build once

chapters.brief: Assemble everything so far into a personal operating system the reader builds in a weekend and improves for years. Include a one-page build plan.

chapters.title: Teams: Shared Prompts, Shared Standards
chapters.brief: Moving from individual to team practice: shared libraries, agreed standards, a common vocabulary, and the difference between a policy that gets read and one that gets used.

How AI raises the quality of fraud — especially payment fraud and impersonation — and what controls actually help: verification channels, callback procedures, and staff training. Prompt injection explained for non-technical readers whose assistants now have tools.

art.title: Ten situations to keep human
labels: Confidential data without a compliant tool

chapters.brief: The chapter that earns the book its credibility. A clear list of situations where the honest answer is to do it yourself, and the professional reasoning behind each.

parts.title: The Next Ten Years of Your Career

chapters.title: What Actually Gets Automated
chapters.brief: Replace the jobs-versus-AI frame with a task-level analysis the reader can apply to their own week. What actually changes in a professional role, what does not, and why the honest answer is neither 'nothing' nor 'everything'. No invented statistics about job losses.

chapters.title: Becoming the Person Who Uses It Well
chapters.brief: Career strategy: the five stages of AI fluency, what to learn at each, and the skills that compound — judgement, verification, domain depth, and the ability to specify work clearly.

chapters.title: The Skills That Get More Valuable

art.title: What rises as generation gets cheap

chapters.brief: The counterintuitive chapter: when producing text becomes cheap, the value moves to deciding what is worth producing and standing behind it. What professionals should invest their learning hours in.

chapters.title: Building an AI-Assisted Practice
chapters.brief: For the reader who wants to build something: how a solo professional or small firm can offer services at a scale that used to require staff, and the honest limits and obligations of doing so. No income promises anywhere in this chapter.
